Case-based learning

Stones, sludge and the pancreas

A case-based session on gallstones, acute cholecystitis, acute pancreatitis and pancreatic adenocarcinoma

MBBS Year 2 | Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary block | 2 hours
Dr Sudha Arumugam, Department of Pathology & Forensic Medicine, MAHSA University

Session plan
Session

How the next two hours run

0 to 10 min

Warm-up: revise the biliary and pancreatic ducts

10 to 50 min

Case 1: Puan Rohana. Gallstones, then acute cholecystitis

50 to 85 min

Each case: read the stem in groups, answer the discussion prompts, then commit to the Quick Check before the answer is revealed.

Learning outcomes
Session

By the end of this session you should be able to

  • Explain how cholesterol and pigment gallstones form, and link each to its risk factors
  • Distinguish biliary colic from acute cholecystitis using clinical, laboratory and pathological features
  • Describe the pathogenesis, morphology and complications of acute calculous cholecystitis
  • List the causes of acute pancreatitis and explain autodigestion, fat necrosis and hypocalcaemia
  • Interpret enzyme results and grade severity of acute pancreatitis
  • Describe the risk factors, precursor lesions, morphology and spread of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
  • Explain painless obstructive jaundice, Courvoisier's sign and Trousseau syndrome
Warm-up
Session

Revise: one exit for bile and pancreatic juice

  • Cystic duct links the gallbladder to the bile ducts
  • CBD meets the main pancreatic duct at the ampulla of Vater
  • Fatty meal: CCK contracts the gallbladder, sphincter of Oddi relaxes
  • Ask: where could one small stone block bile and pancreatic juice together?
Case 1

Puan Rohana's "indigestion"

Gallstones and acute cholecystitis | about 40 minutes

Case 1, part A
Clinical case

A recurring pain after dinner

Puan Rohana is a 44-year-old secondary-school teacher and mother of four. Her BMI is 33 kg/m². Over the last three months she has lost 12 kg on a very low-calorie diet.

She has had three episodes of right upper quadrant and epigastric pain. Each started about an hour after a heavy, oily dinner, lasted 2 to 3 hours and then settled. The pain sometimes spread to the tip of her right shoulder blade.

Seen between attacks: afebrile, abdomen soft and non-tender, no jaundice.

Ultrasound abdomen

  • Multiple mobile echogenic foci in the gallbladder with posterior acoustic shadowing
  • Gallbladder wall 2 mm (normal)
  • Common bile duct 5 mm (normal)
Case 1, part A
Discussion

Discuss in your groups

Q1What is this pain called, and why does it come and go?

Biliary colic. As the gallbladder contracts after a fatty meal (CCK), a stone impacts in the neck or cystic duct. The pain eases when the stone falls back. There is no inflammation of the wall, so no fever, no tenderness and a normal white cell count.

Q2Which of her features raise her risk of gallstones?

Female sex, age in the forties, multiparity (oestrogen and pregnancy), obesity and rapid weight loss. Five risk factors in one patient.

Core content
Core content

Two families of gallstones

Cholesterol stonesBlack pigment stonesBrown pigment stones
Made ofCrystalline cholesterol monohydrate (50 to 100%)Calcium bilirubinate polymers, calcium saltsCalcium bilirubinate with fatty acid soaps
WhereGallbladder onlySterile gallbladder bileInfected intrahepatic or extrahepatic ducts
Typical settingObesity, female, oestrogen, rapid weight loss, Western dietChronic haemolysis (sickle cell, hereditary spherocytosis), cirrhosis, ileal diseaseBiliary infection, liver flukes (Clonorchis), Ascaris; commoner in East Asia
LookPale yellow, hard, often multiple and facetedSmall, black, many, crumblySoft, greasy, brown
X-rayMostly radiolucent (10 to 20% radiopaque)50 to 75% radiopaqueRadiolucent
Core content
Core content

Risk factors: Rohana ticks five boxes

  • About 80% have an identifiable risk factor
  • Mnemonic: female, fat, fertile, forty, plus fasting
  • Oestrogen raises cholesterol uptake and secretion into bile
  • Rapid weight loss: more cholesterol in bile, a gallbladder that does not empty
  • Pigment stones: excess unconjugated bilirubin (haemolysis, infection, ileal disease)
Core content
Core content

How a cholesterol stone forms

1. Supersaturation

Bile carries cholesterol in micelles with bile salts and lecithin. Too much cholesterol, or too little bile salt, and it cannot stay dissolved.

2. Nucleation

Cholesterol monohydrate crystals precipitate. Mucin and calcium salts speed this up.

3. Stasis

A hypomotile gallbladder (pregnancy, fasting, obesity) does not empty, so crystals stay put.

4. Growth

Mucus hypersecretion traps the crystals. They aggregate into sludge, then stones.

Bile is the body's only real route for getting rid of excess cholesterol. That is why the gallbladder pays the price.

Core content
Core content

What the stones look like

Case 1, a second patient
Clinical case

Meanwhile, in the next bed

Puan Rohana, 44

  • Obese, multiparous, rapid weight loss
  • Several pale yellow, faceted stones
  • Recurrent post-prandial pain

Encik Ahmad, 24

  • Hereditary spherocytosis since childhood
  • Splenomegaly, recurrent mild jaundice
  • Ultrasound: many tiny stones; some seen on plain X-ray

Which type of stone does Encik Ahmad have, and why?

Black pigment stones. Chronic haemolysis raises unconjugated bilirubin in bile, which precipitates as calcium bilirubinate in sterile gallbladder bile. Their calcium content explains why some show on a plain film.

Quick check 1Clinical case

Rohana lost 12 kg in three months. Which mechanism best explains how rapid weight loss raised her risk of gallstones?

Mobilised fat sends more cholesterol into bile, and fasting means less CCK-driven emptying, so the gallbladder becomes stagnant. A gives black pigment stones (Ahmad). C gives brown stones in infected ducts. D would lower the risk. E causes pigment stones through altered bilirubin handling, not cholesterol excess.

Quick check 2Clinical case

A plain abdominal X-ray is more likely to show Encik Ahmad's stones than Puan Rohana's. What is the best explanation?

Black pigment stones are rich in calcium salts, and 50 to 75% are radiopaque. Most cholesterol stones are radiolucent, although 10 to 20% carry enough calcium carbonate to show (so B is wrong). Pigment stones are usually small (A), black stones form in the gallbladder (D), and E is not true.

Case 1, part B
Clinical case

Six months later: this time the pain stays

Rohana postponed her operation. She now presents with 18 hours of constant right upper quadrant pain that has not settled, with vomiting and fever.

T 38.4 °C, pulse 104/min. Right upper quadrant tenderness and guarding. On deep palpation under the right costal margin she catches her breath and stops inspiring.

WBC 14.8 × 10⁹/L (neutrophilia), bilirubin 24 µmol/L (ref < 21), ALP 115 U/L, lipase 45 U/L (normal).

Ultrasound abdomen

  • Stone impacted in the gallbladder neck
  • Wall thickened to 6 mm, oedematous
  • Pericholecystic fluid
  • Sonographic Murphy's sign positive
  • CBD not dilated
Case 1, part B
Discussion

Discuss in your groups

Q1How is this different from her earlier attacks? What is the diagnosis?

Pain constant for more than 6 hours, fever, local tenderness and a raised white count: the gallbladder wall is now inflamed. This is acute calculous cholecystitis. The catch in breath on palpation is Murphy's sign.

Q2Her bilirubin is slightly raised but the CBD is normal. Should you worry?

A mild rise can come from oedema and inflammation around the gallbladder. A clearly raised bilirubin or a dilated CBD would suggest a stone has passed into the common bile duct (choledocholithiasis).

Core content
Core content

Acute calculous cholecystitis starts as a chemical injury

  1. 1Stone obstructs the gallbladder neck or cystic duct
  2. 2Mucosal phospholipases turn biliary lecithin into toxic lysolecithin
  3. 3Protective mucus layer breaks down; bile salts act as detergents on the epithelium
  4. 4Prostaglandins released; distension and rising pressure in the lumen
  5. 5Mucosal blood flow falls: ischaemia, inflammation, necrosis

Bacteria (E. coli, Klebsiella, enterococci, anaerobes) are usually a later, secondary event. About 90% of acute cholecystitis is calculous.

Core content
Core content

When there is no stone: acute acalculous cholecystitis

  • About 5 to 12% of cases; patients are usually already very ill
  • Settings: after major non-biliary surgery, severe trauma, extensive burns, sepsis and multi-organ failure, prolonged parenteral nutrition, postpartum
  • Mechanism: stasis (no oral intake), ischaemia (low perfusion of the cystic artery territory), dehydration, secondary infection
  • Gangrene and perforation are more common, and diagnosis is often late because the patient cannot report pain
Core content
Core content

Gross morphology of acute cholecystitis

  • Enlarged and tense
  • Bright red or blotchy violaceous: subserosal haemorrhage
  • Serosa: fibrinous or fibrinopurulent exudate
  • Lumen: stone in the neck in about 90%; cloudy bile with fibrin, blood or pus (empyema)
  • Severe cases: green-black necrotic wall = gangrenous cholecystitis
Core content
Core content

Microscopy of acute cholecystitis

A non-specific acute inflammation: oedema, congestion and haemorrhage, neutrophils through the wall, mucosal ulceration, abscesses and, in severe cases, gangrene.

Core content
Core content

Where gallstones can take her next

  • In the gallbladder: empyema, gangrene, perforation with abscess or bile peritonitis
  • Into the CBD: choledocholithiasis, obstructive jaundice, ascending cholangitis
  • At the ampulla: gallstone pancreatitis (Case 2)
  • Through the wall: cholecystoenteric fistula; a large stone can then obstruct the ileum (gallstone ileus)
  • Sepsis, and over years, chronic cholecystitis
Quick check 3Clinical case

In the first few hours of Rohana's acute calculous cholecystitis, what is the main cause of injury to the gallbladder mucosa?

Obstruction lets mucosal phospholipases form lysolecithin, and bile salts strip the epithelium once the mucus layer fails. Infection (A) is usually secondary and later. Ischaemia comes from distension and pressure, not arterial thrombosis (B). D and E are not part of acute calculous cholecystitis.

Quick check 4Clinical case

A 72-year-old woman with long-standing gallstones has colicky abdominal pain, vomiting and distension. X-ray shows dilated small bowel loops and air in the biliary tree. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A stone has eroded through a cholecystoduodenal fistula (hence air in the biliary tree) and impacted in the ileum, causing obstruction. Empyema and gangrene (A, E) stay within the gallbladder. Cholangitis (B) gives fever, jaundice and pain, not bowel obstruction. C occurs without stones.

Case 2

Two patients, one diagnosis

Acute pancreatitis | about 35 minutes

Case 2
Clinical case

Same night, same emergency department

Puan Rohana, 44

  • Recovered from cholecystitis; still on the surgical waiting list
  • Sudden severe epigastric pain boring through to the back
  • Vomiting, T 37.8 °C, pulse 96/min, BP 128/80

Encik Rajan, 48

  • About 8 cans of strong beer a day for 20 years; binge over a wedding weekend
  • Same pain, more severe; sits leaning forward
  • Pulse 118/min, BP 96/60, RR 26/min

Predict: who is likely to become sicker, and why?

Encik Rajan. Tachycardia, low blood pressure and fast breathing at presentation already point to a systemic inflammatory response and early organ failure.

Case 2
Discussion

Discuss in your groups

Q1What is the diagnosis in both, and what criteria did you use?

Acute pancreatitis. Revised Atlanta: two of three of (1) typical epigastric pain, (2) lipase or amylase at least 3 times the upper limit, (3) imaging features. Both meet the first two, so a CT is not needed to make the diagnosis.

Q2Why is Rohana's ALT so high? What caused each attack?

ALT more than 3 times the upper limit in the first 48 hours points to a gallstone cause: a small stone passing through the ampulla. Rajan's attack follows alcohol.

Q3Do the enzyme levels tell you who is sicker?

No. Rohana has the higher lipase but the milder illness. Severity is judged by organ failure, not enzyme height.

Core content
Core content

Causes of acute pancreatitis

  • Gallstones and alcohol together cause about 80%
  • Metabolic: hypertriglyceridaemia (usually > 11.3 mmol/L), hypercalcaemia
  • Drugs: azathioprine, valproate, thiazides, oestrogens
  • Mechanical: trauma, post-ERCP
  • Genetic: PRSS1, SPINK1, CFTR
  • Vascular: shock, vasculitis. Infection: mumps, Coxsackie virus
  • 10 to 20% remain idiopathic
Core content
Core content

The central event: autodigestion

  • Trypsinogen is activated to trypsin inside the gland
  • Trypsin activates the other proenzymes: phospholipase, elastase
  • It also activates prekallikrein (kinins) and factor XII, switching on clotting and complement
  • Result: oedema, fat necrosis, vessel damage and inflammation
Core content
Core content

Three routes to premature enzyme activation

Duct obstruction

Gallstone or sludge at the ampulla raises duct pressure. Interstitial oedema impairs blood flow and lipase-rich fluid leaks into tissue. (Rohana)

Primary acinar injury

Alcohol, some drugs, viruses, ischaemia and trauma damage acinar cells directly.

Defective intracellular transport

Proenzymes are sent to lysosomes instead of the apical membrane. Lysosomal hydrolases activate trypsinogen. (Rajan)

Alcohol works through several routes at once: increased protein-rich secretion that plugs ducts, sphincter of Oddi contraction, direct acinar toxicity and oxidative stress.

Quick check 5Clinical case

Which enzyme is the key trigger for autodigestion in both patients, because it activates the others?

Trypsin activates the other proenzymes as well as the kinin, clotting and complement systems. Lipase (A) causes fat necrosis and amylase (B) is only a marker. Elastase (D) destroys vessel walls and phospholipase (E) damages membranes, but neither starts the cascade.

Core content
Core content

Morphology: the five basic lesions

  • Microvascular leak causing oedema
  • Fat necrosis by lipases
  • Acute inflammation
  • Proteolytic destruction of the parenchyma
  • Destruction of blood vessels (elastase), with interstitial haemorrhage

Two clinical forms

  • Interstitial oedematous: most patients, gland swollen but perfused (Rohana)
  • Necrotising: about 5 to 10%; parenchymal and peripancreatic necrosis, often haemorrhagic (Rajan)
Core content
Core content

Gross: haemorrhage and chalky fat necrosis

  • Swollen gland with areas of haemorrhagic necrosis
  • Chalky white spots in peripancreatic fat, omentum and mesentery
  • Saponification: released fatty acids bind calcium to form insoluble calcium soaps
  • This is where Rajan's calcium went
Core content
Core content

Microscopy: enzymatic fat necrosis

Also look for necrotic acini, ducts and vessels, haemorrhage and neutrophils.

Case 2, day 2 to 4
Clinical case

Their paths separate

Puan Rohana

  • Pain settles over 3 days
  • Eating normally by day 3
  • No organ failure
  • Laparoscopic cholecystectomy before discharge

Encik Rajan

  • SpO₂ 88%, bilateral lung infiltrates
  • Creatinine still rising; needs fluids and support beyond 48 h
  • CT day 4: more than 30% of the gland not enhancing, peripancreatic collections
  • Admitted to ICU

Grade each patient's severity. Why remove Rohana's gallbladder during this admission?

Revised Atlanta: Rohana is mild (no organ failure, no complications). Rajan is severe (organ failure lasting more than 48 hours). Rohana's gallbladder comes out early because the risk of another attack of gallstone pancreatitis is high while the stones remain.

Core content
Core content

Reading the laboratory results

TestWhat it tells you
AmylaseRises within 24 hours and falls in 3 to 5 days. Also raised in parotitis, perforated ulcer, bowel ischaemia, renal failure
LipaseRises a little later and stays up longer. More specific for the pancreas; the preferred test
ALT > 3 × ULNSuggests a gallstone cause
Low calciumSaponification in fat necrosis; a poor prognostic sign
CRP > 150 mg/L at 48 hSuggests severe disease
Rising urea, haematocritFluid loss into the retroperitoneum; worse outcome
Contrast CTNot needed for diagnosis. Best after 72 hours to look for necrosis and collections
Core content
Core content

Complications

Local

  • Acute peripancreatic fluid collection
  • Pseudocyst: after about 4 weeks, walled by granulation and fibrous tissue, no epithelial lining
  • Walled-off necrosis; infected necrosis and abscess
  • Haemorrhage; splenic vein thrombosis

Systemic

  • SIRS and shock
  • ARDS: circulating phospholipase damages surfactant
  • Acute kidney injury, DIC
  • Hypocalcaemia, hyperglycaemia
  • Distant (subcutaneous) fat necrosis
Quick check 6Clinical case

Encik Rajan's serum calcium is 1.78 mmol/L on day 2. What is the best explanation?

Lipase releases fatty acids that combine with calcium as insoluble soaps (saponification). B does not happen. C and D can lower calcium over time but do not explain a sharp fall on day 2. Dilution (E) is minor and would also lower other values.

Quick check 7Clinical case

Six weeks later Rajan has early satiety and a vague epigastric mass. CT shows a 9 cm round fluid collection with a thick wall next to the pancreas. What would a biopsy of the wall most likely show?

This is a pseudocyst: necrotic material walled off by granulation and fibrous tissue, with no epithelium (hence pseudo). A is a mucinous cystic neoplasm, B a serous cystadenoma, D an epidermoid or dermoid cyst, and E invasive adenocarcinoma.

Case 3

Mr Tan turns yellow

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma | about 25 minutes

Case 3
Clinical case

Two months of yellow eyes and itching

Mr Tan, a 67-year-old retired lorry driver, has smoked for 40 pack-years. Type 2 diabetes was diagnosed 6 months ago; he is not overweight and has no family history.

For two months: yellow eyes, generalised itching, dark urine and pale stools. He has lost 9 kg. A dull epigastric ache goes through to his back and is worse at night.

Last month a painful red cord appeared on his left forearm, settled, then another on his right calf.

Examination: deep jaundice, scratch marks, a palpable, non-tender gallbladder.

Discussion

Discuss in your groups

Q1Why can you feel Mr Tan's gallbladder but not Rohana's?

Courvoisier's sign: a palpable, non-tender gallbladder in a jaundiced patient makes stones unlikely. Stone-bearing gallbladders are usually scarred and cannot distend. Slow malignant obstruction of the distal CBD (head of pancreas, ampulla, distal bile duct) lets it fill up.

Q2What links his new diabetes, his red cords and his raised INR to the tumour?

New diabetes in a thin older adult can be an early sign of pancreatic cancer. The red cords are migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau syndrome). The INR is up because no bile reaches the gut, so vitamin K is not absorbed.

Core content
Core content

Who gets pancreatic cancer?

  • Smoking: the strongest environmental factor, about twice the risk
  • Age over 60, obesity, long-standing diabetes
  • Chronic pancreatitis
  • Inherited: BRCA2, CDKN2A (familial melanoma), Lynch syndrome, Peutz-Jeghers, hereditary pancreatitis (PRSS1)
  • Third commonest cause of cancer death in the USA; overall 5-year survival about 13%
Core content
Core content

From PanIN to invasive cancer

  • Precursor: pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanIN) in small ducts, graded low or high grade
  • KRAS: early, in more than 90%
  • CDKN2A (p16): the most often inactivated tumour suppressor, about 95%
  • Late: TP53 (50 to 70%) and SMAD4 (about 55%)
  • Other precursors: IPMN and mucinous cystic neoplasm
Core content
Core content

Gross: a hard, grey-white, ill-defined mass

  • Site: head 60%, body 15%, tail 5%, diffuse 20%
  • Hard, grey-white, stellate, poorly defined
  • Head tumours obstruct the distal CBD: jaundice and a distended gallbladder
  • Body and tail tumours stay silent until large and spread
Core content
Core content

Microscopy

  • Moderately to poorly differentiated infiltrating glands, often mucin-producing
  • Intense desmoplastic (fibrotic) stroma: why the tumour feels hard
  • Perineural invasion, within and beyond the gland
  • Lymphatic and vascular invasion common
Core content
Core content

How it behaves and spreads

  • Silent until it involves nearby structures
  • Pain: retroperitoneal nerve invasion. Obstructive jaundice with head tumours
  • Weight loss, anorexia, new diabetes
  • Trousseau syndrome (about 10%): tumour procoagulants
  • Spread: duodenum, stomach, spleen, colon; regional nodes; liver, lungs, bone; peritoneum
Core content
Core content

Diagnosis and the limits of CA19-9

  • Pancreatic-protocol contrast CT to stage the tumour
  • EUS with fine-needle aspiration or biopsy for tissue
  • CA19-9: useful to follow response and recurrence, not for screening
  • False positives in obstructive jaundice and cholangitis; Lewis-antigen-negative people cannot make it
  • Only about 15 to 20% are resectable (Whipple procedure) at presentation
Quick check 8Clinical case

Which genetic change is usually the earliest, and present in more than 90% of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas?

KRAS mutation appears early in low-grade PanIN and is found in over 90% of cancers. TP53 (A) and SMAD4 (C) are late events. BRCA2 (D) is a germline risk in a small minority. APC (E) is the gatekeeper of colorectal, not pancreatic, carcinogenesis.

Quick check 9Clinical case

Which finding in Mr Tan most strongly argues against a stone in the common bile duct as the cause of his jaundice?

Courvoisier's sign. A, B, C and E occur in any obstructive jaundice, whatever the cause. A distended, non-tender gallbladder suggests slow malignant obstruction of the distal duct, because stone-bearing gallbladders are usually fibrosed.

Quick check 10Clinical case

What best explains the painful red cords that appeared, one after another, on Mr Tan's arm and leg?

Trousseau syndrome: tumour-derived procoagulants (tissue factor, mucins) cause thromboses that come and go at different sites. It occurs in about 10% of patients. A, C and D do not produce this migrating pattern, and E needs a cannula at each site.

Self-assessment 1

A 35-year-old woman with poorly controlled diabetes has severe epigastric pain radiating to the back. Lipase is 12 times the upper limit. Her serum looks milky and triglycerides are 25 mmol/L. She does not drink and ultrasound shows no gallstones. What is the most likely cause?

Triglycerides above about 11.3 mmol/L can cause acute pancreatitis, and poorly controlled diabetes is a common setting. She does not drink (A) and has no stones (B). Nothing suggests hypercalcaemia (D) or viral infection (E).

Self-assessment 2

A 60-year-old man is on day 10 in ICU after 40% burns. He develops a new fever and right upper quadrant tenderness. Ultrasound shows a distended gallbladder with a thick wall and no stones. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Critical illness, burns, fasting and poor perfusion cause gallbladder stasis and ischaemia without stones. Biliary colic (A) and empyema from a stone (D) need stones. C needs a duct stone and usually jaundice. E would give a raised lipase and epigastric pain.

Self-assessment 3

Which feature on CT separates necrotising from interstitial oedematous acute pancreatitis?

Non-enhancing parenchyma means tissue with no blood supply, which is necrosis. Enlargement (A) and fat stranding (B) occur in both forms. D and E do not define the type.

Take-home
Session

Take-home points

  • Cholesterol stones: supersaturation, nucleation, stasis. Pigment stones: excess unconjugated bilirubin
  • Colic comes and goes; cholecystitis stays, with fever, tenderness and Murphy's sign
  • Acute cholecystitis begins as a sterile chemical injury; bacteria arrive later
  • Acute pancreatitis is autodigestion triggered by trypsin. Gallstones and alcohol cause about 80%
  • Severity depends on organ failure, not enzyme level. Low calcium means fat necrosis
  • Painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder: think head of pancreas cancer. KRAS early, desmoplasia and perineural invasion
